In this lab session, we are transforming a corpus of inaugural speeches of US Presidents into a Document-Feature-matrix. We are not yet worrying about creating a corpus - that will come when we talk about finding and importing your own texts. This corpus comes included with quanteda and can be loaded just by assigning it to a variable:

```{r}
#| message: False

library(quanteda)
speeches <- data_corpus_inaugural
```

We will use some functions that were not covered in the lecture. Most of the tasks we are applying here can be found in the [quanteda tutorial](https://tutorials.quanteda.io/) by Müller and Watanabe.

## Working with the corpus

1) Display the head of the corpus itself and of the document variables.

```{r}
head(speeches)
docvars(speeches) |> head()

# Inline alternative / Base R style:
# head(docvars(speeches))
```

2) Create a new corpus that only contains speeches made in the 21st century. Check how many documents are in the new corpus (there should be 7). Print the number of tokens in each speech.

```{r}
speeches_21 <- corpus_subset(speeches,
                             Year >= 2000)

ndoc(speeches_21)
ntoken(speeches_21)
```
(The deprecation warning points out it would be better to use the tokenizer function that we get to know in the next bit. This is true because it gives us more control over how the tokenizer behaves. In general, we rarely use this function outside of illustration purposes anyway.)

3) Create a new corpus that takes the 21st century speeches and reshapes them to the sentence level. How many tokens are in the longest sentence in the corpus?

```{r}
sentences_21 <- corpus_reshape(speeches_21,
                               to = "sentences")

ntoken(sentences_21) |> 
  max() 
```

The longest sentence is 98 tokens long.

## Tokenization

4) Take the 21st century corpus (with the documents being full speeches). Tokenize it while removing punctuation. Then remove all English stopwords as well. Compare the length of the tokenized speeches to the number of tokens you got in 2).

```{r}
toks_21 <- tokens(speeches_21,
                  remove_punct = T) |> 
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"))

ntoken(toks_21)
```

Every speech loses a bit more than half its tokens when applying basic pre-processing steps. This shows just how much of a speech is punctuation and stop words!

5) Take any instance of "United States" in the speeches and compound the token to "United_States".

```{r}
toks_21 <- tokens_compound(toks_21,
                           pattern = phrase("United States"))
```

## DFM

6) Create a document-feature-matrix of the token object you have made. Trim it by deleting all features with less than 10 occurrences. Print its first rows with ```head()```.

```{r}
dfmat <- dfm(toks_21) |> 
  dfm_trim(min_termfreq = 10)
head(dfmat)
```

7) What are the 10 most common features in the texts?

```{r}
topfeatures(dfmat, n = 10)
```

8) Create a document-feature-matrix of all speeches in the corpus. How do the 10 most common features across all years differ from the 21st century corpus?

```{r}
dfmat_all <- speeches |>
  tokens(remove_punct = T) |> 
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) |> 
  tokens_compound(
    pattern = phrase("United States")
  ) |> 
  dfm() |> 
  dfm_trim(min_termfreq = 10)

topfeatures(dfmat_all, n = 10)
```
"People" and "Government" stand out as being much more common, as is "World". On the other hand, "Nation" becomes less relevant compared to 21st century speeches. Based on these top features alone, we might suspect that speeches have become more patriotic or even nationalist, compared to being focused more on the American people and their place in the world. However, drawing such conclusions from just 10 features would of course be very overly ambitious!
